newsitem.title: INDIA: ISO urges sugar producers to halt expansion.
newsitem.headline: ISO urges sugar producers to halt expansion.

text.p: The head of the International Sugar Organisation (ISO), worried that a third year of surplus global sugar supplies will hurt prices, on Wednesday suggested a halt to production increases to stabilise the market.

ISO executive director Peter Baron, attending a three-day international sugar conference in New Delhi, told Reuters early indications showed that 1996/97 (October-September) crop year would be the third in a row that produced a sugar surplus.

"Producers have to consider whether they should be cautious about expansion programmes, production increase or whether they should not, whether it would be wiser to give the market a certain period of rest and try to calm the market down by not producing more," Baron said.
He did not give a forecast for world sugar supply and demand in the crop year beginning on October 1 but said production would outstrip demand, putting prices under pressure over the next six months.
"We cannot exclude the (raw sugar) prices go to 10 or even below 10 cents a pound, compared to 12 cents for the time being," Baron said. "I think the prices will react over the next six months."
But he expected prices to improve over coming years because the market for commodities was cyclical.
He forecast an average two to three percent annual growth in sugar consumption in Asia and a one to two percent growth in other parts of the world.

The ISO, an inter-governmental organisation based in London with 46 member countries, estimates world sugar production in 1995/96 at 123 million tonnes and consumption at 117.5 million, leaving a surplus of 5.5 million.
Baron said the ISO did not want to interfere on policy matters, leaving member-countries to make their own decisions.
"We tell them 'Look, the market is in surplus and that will be for quite sometime and so be prepared the market may react in a way which is not desirable to you'."
Baron said the ISO would advise importing countries to use the opportunity of lower prices to buy.
He said developing countries, accounting for 70 percent of world sugar imports, might be tempted to buy more due to lower prices.
"It could be possible, due to lower prices, the imports may strengthen. This could alleviate a little bit of pressure on the market," Baron said.
He said consumption in Asia would grow faster than elsewhere. "Asia plays the music, here is the place where sugar policies and markets are decided."
